title: 3 YEARS WITHOUT INJURIES: How I bulletproofed myself (and how you can do it too)
summary: He explains how he went from constantly hurt to three years injury-free. His methods: using reps in reserve selectively, lift by lift, and treating saved reps as an investment; banishing exercises that don't suit him to an 'exercise graveyard'; rotating lifts to vary joint angles; stimulating rather than annihilating the muscle; and practising patience and listening to his body.
claims: Pain is a warning sign of injury to come, not something to romantically train through
Between a lifter who always pushes through pain and is often out of commission and a more cautious one who keeps training, the cautious one goes further
Reps in reserve is not the enemy of failure; use it to pick your battles so you can go to failure where it matters
If you put 100% into everything, it isn't really 100%; going to failure on every set fails to allocate resources
Every movement has a 'red zone', a disadvantaged range that stimulates the muscle most but carries the most risk; enter it with caution
Most gym injuries happen in the last few reps of heavy sets, when fatigue is highest
The last two grinding reps are not magical; four reps of a planned six on squats is still high-quality tonnage
Cut the last reps in one or two sessions out of four or five; occasional failure lifters lose little but are injured far less
Injuries with heavy weights are much more severe than injuries during warm-ups with light weights
Before grinding reps, ask whether they are worth the risk that day; if not, keep them in reserve
Saved reps can be reinvested as extra back-off sets on safer variations, making up for lost tonnage and more
Fighting for 2-3 extra heavy deadlift reps can cost the ability to do another hip hinge afterward, losing tonnage and adding injury risk
Set RIR per lift: e.g. RIR 2 on deadlifts but RIR 0 on Romanian deadlifts or hyperextensions, which are lower risk
Curls and bench press (with safeties) can always go to failure since the risk is low; RIR matters most on lower-body lifts
Beginners to RIR should start with one hip hinge or knee-flexion lift, not apply 2 RIR to the whole program
He used to get hurt on squats grinding 3-4 extra reps; after cutting them he has had no squat injury in three years
If a rep would become a good morning, keep it in reserve and spend the energy on a later quad exercise like leg extensions
Put exercises that cause pain or don't suit your build in an 'exercise graveyard' and stop doing them
He is stubborn and has kept doing lifts that didn't suit him for years; clinging to them is the sunk cost fallacy
Muscle and strength built on a dropped lift carry over to a replacement better suited to you
Rotations let you keep working a muscle without repeating the exact same movement
As an ex-powerlifter he deadlifted conventionally every 4-5 days for fear of losing strength; a bodybuilder only needs to train the hip hinge every 2-3 days
Overuse injuries come from training a muscle with the same angles, weight and stance every time, not from the frequency itself; a quad can take training every 48 hours if the stance varies
Stimulate, don't annihilate: work the muscle, not the tendons and joints around it
Tendon pain the day after an arm session means you overtaxed the tendon; tendinitis inflammation can last weeks to months while the muscle recovers fast
The lower back 'pump' after deadlifts is often SI joint pain, since there is no muscle there; stop before it sets in so muscles fatigue before joints
He ignored rib pain until a rib snapped; there are no freak accidents, injuries come with signs
Hitting legs every 48 hours beats hammering them every 10 days; bro-split leg days produce poor legs
Without RIR you lose control and the rep range controls you; failure shouldn't mean grinding as many reps as possible every time
Patience prevents injuries: like the train that slows on curves, slower progress without derailing goes further
Every time he got injured it was from impatience about hitting a target weight, costing him months
He now senses before a set when it will injure him; when your instinct warns you, take a step back since the worst case is a wasted set
Three years without tendon pain probably saved his relationship with lifting
Pain-free bodybuilding is the best way to keep getting bigger as you age
exercises: stop the last grinding reps if form breaks
cutting grind reps ended his squat injuries
high-risk, fatiguing lift; save reps for other hinges
less risky hinge to push to failure
failing a rep is low risk
spend reserved energy directly on quads
